An ascot is a type of neckwear — a wide, flat, soft piece of cloth worn around the neck, usually tucked inside the collar of a shirt or draped loosely over it.

Think of a regular necktie, but much wider and flatter — almost like a broad scarf or a loosely folded band of fabric. It doesn't hang down like a standard tie. Instead, it wraps around the neck and the two wide ends cross over each other and rest on the chest, sitting right at the collar or just below the throat. It has a soft, flowing, elegant appearance.

The ascot is usually:

  • Tucked inside the shirt — pulled through the collar and nestled between the shirt buttons and the collar, with the fabric puffing out softly
  • Or draped loosely over the shirt, with the ends folded flat against the chest
  • Sometimes secured with a tie pin or brooch to keep it in place
  • Worn with the top button of the shirt often left open so the cloth can spread naturally

It is not knotted the way a regular tie is. The crossing and folding is done loosely, giving it that relaxed but refined look.
How it differs from a regular necktie and a bow tie

A regular necktie is long and narrow, hangs straight down the front of your shirt, and is knotted tightly at the collar. An ascot is much wider, shorter, and draped — not knotted. It sits high on the chest near the collar, rather than hanging.

A bow tie is tied into a neat small bow at the collar. An ascot is wider, softer, and much more loosely arranged — it looks more like a flowing cloth than a rigid, structured accessory.
What kind of fabric it's made of

Ascots are traditionally made from fine, smooth, often slightly shiny fabrics like silk, satin, or fine cotton. They may be plain (a single colour), striped, or patterned. The fabric choice adds to their elegant, polished look.
What occasions and contexts it belongs to

Historically, ascots were formal daytime neckwear, worn mostly by upper-class men at events like horse races, garden parties, and formal brunches or luncheons. In the British tradition especially, ascots were considered the appropriate neckwear for morning dress — a formal daytime suit. The famous Royal Ascot horse racing event in England is so associated with this neckwear that the race meet itself takes its name from it (or vice versa — the two are deeply linked in British culture).

Over time, ascots moved beyond strictly formal wear. In the 20th century, they became popular as a leisurely, casual-yet-sophisticated accessory among artists, actors, and well-dressed men who wanted to look stylish without the stiffness of a full suit and tie. You might see them worn with an open-collared shirt, a blazer, or a smoking jacket.

When someone wears an ascot today, the general impression it gives is:

  • Refined and old-fashioned — it evokes an era of leisure, wealth, and careful dressing
  • Artistic or theatrical — it's associated with actors, writers, and personalities who want to look distinctive
  • Occasionally ironic or playful — because it's so strongly tied to a certain old-fashioned elegance, some people wear it with a sense of self-awareness or humour

In pop culture, the ascot is often used in cartoons and films to signal that a character is wealthy, posh, eccentric, or stylishly old-world. (Fred from Scooby-Doo famously wears an ascot.)

Though ascots are most strongly associated with men's fashion, women wear them too — typically as a stylish, soft accessory tied around the neck with a shirt or blouse, giving a vintage or editorial look. In women's fashion, the line between an ascot and a neck scarf can blur, but the key feature remains: it's wider and more structured than a simple scarf, and worn specifically around the collar area of a shirt or dress.

An ascot is a wide, soft, flat piece of elegant cloth worn folded or draped around the neck, tucked into or over a shirt collar. It is not knotted like a tie but arranged loosely. It signals refinement, old-world sophistication, and a certain deliberate stylishness — sitting somewhere between formal neckwear and a decorative accessory.
